content:
In December 1950 a custody case over a thirteen-year-old girl ended in three days of rioting in Singapore. The girl was born Maria Hertogh to a Dutch Catholic family and raised as Nadra, or Natrah, by a Malay Muslim woman. The case is still told in two opposite ways: as a Muslim mob attacking Europeans, or as a colonial court tearing a Muslim child from her mother.

Both versions leave out half of the record. The court's own words, the press that inflamed the city and the deaths on both sides belong in the same account.

This article aims to provide context to the case, insha'Allah, in seven facts from the court record, the official history and the scholarship. The Quran holds every part of the story to one standard: "stand out firmly for justice, as witnesses to Allah, even as against yourselves" (4:135).[1]

Huberdina Maria Hertogh was born on 24 March 1937 in Cimahi, near Bandung in Java, then part of the Dutch East Indies. Her father, Adrianus Petrus Hertogh, was a sergeant in the Royal Netherlands East Indies Army; her mother was Adeline Hunter.[2]

During the Japanese occupation her parents were interned. In the first days of 1943 the child went to stay with Che Aminah binte Mohamed, a Malay woman from Kemaman in Terengganu and a friend of the family.[2] What was agreed at that time became the centre of the dispute, and her mother and Che Aminah gave the courts different accounts of it.[2]

Che Aminah raised her in Kemaman under the name Nadra binte Ma'arof, a Muslim and a Malay speaker.[3] By 1950 she had lived with Che Aminah for seven years, and Malay was her language.[2]

To the Malay community she was a Muslim girl raised by a Muslim mother. To her natal parents she was a Dutch child they had lost in the war. Each side had a real claim, and the courts had to decide between them.

In April 1950 the High Court in Singapore placed her with the Social Welfare Department pending a decision. On 19 May, after a hearing of fifteen minutes, it gave custody to the Hertoghs.[2] Che Aminah appealed, and in July the Court of Appeal set the order aside for defects in the way the Dutch consulate had represented the father, and returned the girl to her.[2]

The case was a custody dispute decided under colonial law. The question of her religion followed from the question of who had the right to decide it.

On 1 August 1950, at the age of thirteen, she was married to Mansoor Adabi, a twenty-one-year-old trainee teacher, in a nikah gantung, a marriage to be consummated when both were of age.[2] The Hertoghs went back to court.

Justice Algernon Brown gave judgment on 2 December 1950.[4] He found the marriage "a manoeuvre designed to prejudice these proceedings", though he was "satisfied that the child was neither forced nor tricked into it". He held it void because she was under age by the law of her father's domicile, and added: "since her father had not ... consented to her becoming a Muslim, whatever the child may say and whatever ceremonies and teaching she may have undergone, she is not in the eyes of this court a Muslim."[2]

That last sentence was the one Muslims in Malaya heard. A court had declared that a girl who prayed as a Muslim was not one.

She was placed in the Convent of the Good Shepherd while the appeal was heard, and newspapers published photographs of her there, among them one of her kneeling before a statue of Mary.[2] To Muslims who had followed the case, the pictures looked like a conversion being forced on a Muslim child.

The coverage on both sides inflamed the city. The Quran's rule for such moments is the first one any newspaper should follow: "If a wicked person comes to you with any news, ascertain the truth, lest ye harm people unwittingly" (49:6).[1]

On the morning of 11 December a crowd gathered over the case, swelling to between 2,000 and 3,000, and the violence did not subside until 13 December. The official count is that "18 people died and 173 were injured."[5]

The dead included seven Europeans or Eurasians, two police officers and nine rioters shot by police or troops.[2] Many of the dead had no part in the case. Islam condemns that without qualification: "And let not the hatred of others to you make you swerve to wrong and depart from justice. Be just: that is next to piety" (5:8).[1]

She was taken to the Netherlands, where she lived as Bertha Hertogh. She returned to Malaysia in 1999 for a Dutch television documentary, and died in Huijbergen on 8 July 2009.[2]

Historians still debate the case. Tom Eames Hughes wrote its first full history in 1980, and Syed Muhd Khairudin Aljunied returned to it in 2009 as a study of colonialism, violence and Muslims in Southeast Asia.[6]

The bottom line

The Natrah case was a custody dispute between two families, each with a real claim, decided by colonial courts that ruled a Muslim-raised girl was not a Muslim because her father had not consented. Photographs of her in a convent inflamed the press, and riots in December 1950 left eighteen dead, many of them people with no part in the case.

The record supports neither slogan. Muslims had a grievance against a court that disregarded the faith she had been raised in, and no grievance excuses killing the innocent. The Quran's standard covers both: justice "even as against yourselves" (4:135).[1] Allahu alam.

Notes

  1. Quran 4:135; 5:8; 49:6, translated by A. Yusuf Ali.
  2. "Maria Hertogh", English Wikipedia, on her birth, family and adoption, the custody hearings of 1950, the marriage, the judgment of Justice Brown (quoted from Re M. H. Hertogh, an Infant: Hertogh v. Amina binte Mohamed and Others), the convent photographs, the casualties and her later life.
  3. "Maria Hertogh Riots on 11 Dec 1950", SG101, Government of Singapore, on her name Nadra binte Ma'arof and Che Aminah.
  4. Tom Eames Hughes, Tangled Worlds: The Story of Maria Hertogh (Singapore: Institute of Southeast Asian Studies, 1980), chapter "The Judgement of Mr Justice Brown, 2 December 1950".
  5. "Maria Hertogh Riots on 11 Dec 1950", SG101, Government of Singapore, citing the National Library Board's Infopedia for the figures.
  6. Syed Muhd Khairudin Aljunied, Colonialism, Violence and Muslims in Southeast Asia: The Maria Hertogh Controversy and Its Aftermath (London: Routledge, 2009), reviewed by Clive S. Kessler, American Historical Review 116, no. 4 (2011), pp. 1111–1112; Hughes, Tangled Worlds.
